policy_title: End 'woke' policing and reform police oversight

verdict.plain: Scrapping DE&I roles removes the main institutional mechanism for addressing documented racial disparities in policing — such as stop-and-search rates — which risks worsening equal treatment for minority communities. The IOPC overhaul is too vague to reliably offset this.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether removing formal DE&I structures would cause racial disproportionality in police practices to materially worsen, or whether other accountability mechanisms would partially compensate.

claims.claim: The policy commits to scrapping all DE&I roles and regulations in policing and overhauling the IOPC for greater public accountability.
claims.quote: Reform UK will scrap all Diversity, Equality and Inclusion (DE&I) roles and regulations to stop 'two-tier policing' and overhaul the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) to make the police complaints system more accountable to the public.

claims.claim: Black people are six to nine times more likely to be stopped and searched than white people, suggesting racial disparity in policing practice.
claims.quote: Black people being six to nine times more likely to be stopped and searched than white people, and disproportionately subjected to force, including Tasers

claims.claim: Data on stop-and-search, use of weapons, and deaths in custody shows racially minoritised groups are disproportionately affected by police violence.
claims.quote: existing data on stop-and-search, use of weapons, and deaths in custody demonstrates that women, queer people, and racially minoritised groups are disproportionately affected by police violence

claims.claim: Ethnic minority officers remain significantly under-represented in the police, particularly in senior ranks.
claims.quote: Asian people made up 3.8% of officers compared to 10.1% of the working-age population, and Black people made up 1.3% of officers compared to 4.4% of the working-age population

claims.claim: A retiring Chief Constable warned that abolishing DE&I policies threatens to take policing backwards, arguing dedicated resources are needed to close a confidence gap and ensure equitable service.
claims.quote: dismissed Reform UK's promise to abolish equality and diversity policies as "ludicrous" and warned that it "threatens to take policing and society backwards"

claims.quote: Without such initiatives, disproportionality in the use of police powers, which has remained static despite DE&I efforts in some forces, might worsen or become harder to explain and address

claims.quote: any "two-tier" experience of policing is due to racial disparities in practices like stop and search, not the result of DE&I policies themselves

claims.claim: Public confidence in the police complaints system is already low, with 48% not confident in fair treatment of complaints.
claims.quote: 48% of the public were not confident in the police dealing fairly with complaints, compared to 42% who were confident

claims.quote: there is a general consensus among government, the IOPC itself, and other stakeholders that reforms are needed to improve timeliness, efficiency, and public confidence

verdict.rationale: On O9, the dominant effect of this policy is the removal of DE&I structures that currently act as the main institutional response to documented racial disparities in policing. The evidence base shows substantial and persistent disproportionality: Black people face stop-and-search at six to nine times the rate of white people, and racially minoritised groups are disproportionately affected by police violence. Ethnic minority representation in the police — especially at senior ranks — remains well below population share. These disparities represent an equal-treatment deficit, and DE&I mechanisms are the primary policy lever currently directed at them. Removing those mechanisms, absent a credible alternative instrument to address the same disparities, is projected by senior police professionals and expert bodies to worsen or entrench unequal treatment of minorities. The counter-claim — that DE&I itself creates 'two-tier' policing disadvantaging the majority — is asserted by the policy and its supporters but is not supported by independent institutional evidence in the provided units; the evidence instead attributes disproportionate outcomes to systemic disparities, not to DE&I programmes. On the IOPC component: there is genuine consensus that reform is needed, and improving accountability and due process in the complaints system is directionally positive for O9. However, the policy commits only to 'overhaul' without specifying mechanism, budget, or statutory instrument. Under the soft-verb rule, this aspirational commitment cannot earn an 'improves' signal. At best it is neutral-to-uncertain. The net verdict is therefore 'worsens': the concrete commitment (scrap DE&I) removes equal-treatment mechanisms in a context of documented minority disadvantage, while the vague commitment (overhaul IOPC) provides insufficient offsetting signal. Magnitude is moderate because the disproportionality is persistent and large, but the actual marginal effect of removing DE&I programmes (given their partial effectiveness) carries real uncertainty.

blocking_issues.detail: Claim 2 (Black people 6–9× more likely to be stopped and searched) is labelled 'measurable' and cited solely from E5 (nationalcentrefordiversity.com), which appears to be an advocacy/interest source. Per sourcing rules, advocacy sources may not be the sole basis for a verdict claim presented as factual baseline. The directional disparity is corroborated by E7 (LSE blog) and government workforce data in E9, but the specific 6–9× figure has no independent government or academic citation in the evidence set. The claim should either be downgraded to 'projected' or a government statistical source (e.g. Home Office stop-and-search data) should be added.

verifier.notes: The verdict is otherwise well-structured. Tier separation is maintained: stated claims quote the manifesto verbatim, measurable baselines use government/academic sources (E7, E9, E16, E35), and projected claims are appropriately hedged. No tier_integrity violations detected beyond the E5 issue noted above. Magnitude/time_horizon are consistent with the evidence weight. No lever_leakage: DE&I removal is judged by its modelled effect on equal-treatment outcomes, not as a policy lever in itself. No party_blind issues: the counter-claim from Reform UK supporters is engaged on its evidential merits rather than attributed to motive or ideology. No false_balance: the 'worsens' direction is supported by multiple independent claims; the counter-claim is acknowledged but correctly noted as lacking independent institutional backing. The IOPC uncertainty is handled appropriately — the soft-verb rule is applied and no 'improves' signal is claimed. Publication can proceed with the E5 sourcing caveat resolved.

evidence.snippet: Reform UK will scrap all Diversity, Equality and Inclusion (DE&I) roles and regulations to stop 'two-tier policing' and overhaul the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) to make the police complaints system more accountable to the public.

Farage points to police race-action plans and anti-racism commitments as evidence, citing testimony from current and former officers who feel they are receiving "indoctrination" about "white privilege" and "institutionally racist organizations"
Reform UK's Home Affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, has stated that a Reform government would pass an Equal Treatment Act to remove all race action and DE&I programs from policing

Serena Kennedy, a retiring Chief Constable of Merseyside police, dismissed Reform UK's promise to abolish equality and diversity policies as "ludicrous" and warned that it "threatens to take policing and society backwards"
Dedicated resources for DE&I are, in her view, essential to close this "confidence gap" and ensure equitable service

Instead, they contend that the real divide lies in systemic racial disparities, with clear statistical evidence of Black people being six to nine times more likely to be stopped and searched than white people, and disproportionately subjected to force, including Tasers
This suggests an institutional bias rather than preferential treatment for minorities

The LSE article highlights that existing data on stop-and-search, use of weapons, and deaths in custody demonstrates that women, queer people, and racially minoritised groups are disproportionately affected by police violence

As of March 31, 2024, ethnic minority officers (excluding white minorities) constituted 8.4% of the workforce, a proportion that had been increasing since 2007 (4.7%) until 2024, when it remained steady

For instance, in 2024, White people made up 91.6% of police officers (where ethnicity was known) compared to 80.7% of the working-age population, while Asian people made up 3.8% of officers compared to 10.1% of the working-age population, and Black people made up 1.3% of officers compared to 4.4% of the working-age population
Representation of minority ethnic officers was even lower among senior ranks (chief inspector or above) at 6.5% compared with 9.0% of constables

For example, Essex Police reported that since the implementation of their DE&I board, female representation among police officers rose from 33% to over 38%, and ethnic minority representation increased from 3.2% to 4.06%
The House of Commons Library has also published briefings on police service strength and diversity, highlighting the under-representation of Black and minority ethnic people in police forces
In 2016, the Home Affairs Committee found the "painfully slow" progress in BME representation "unacceptable" and called for "urgent and radical action"
Experts argue that dedicated resources are necessary to address existing confidence gaps and ensure equitable service delivery
Without such initiatives, disproportionality in the use of police powers, which has remained static despite DE&I efforts in some forces, might worsen or become harder to explain and address

The IOPC's 2024/25 Public Perceptions Tracker revealed that while awareness of the IOPC is at its highest since its creation, 48% of the public were not confident in the police dealing fairly with complaints, compared to 42% who were confident

Surveys also indicate a general loss of public confidence in the police, with the proportion of people who thought the police were doing a good job falling from an average of 70% in 2020 to 47% by April 2023
In October 2024, the Home Secretary announced measures, many of which were welcomed by the IOPC Director General Rachel Watson, to improve timeliness and clarity

These include:
*   Aligning the threshold for IOPC referrals of officers to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) with the test used by police for referring cases involving the public
This aims to avoid clogging the system and allow swifter resolution of referred cases
*   Allowing the IOPC to send cases to the CPS for prosecution prior to completing their final investigation report, thereby speeding up processes
*   Placing the IOPC's Victims' Right to Review policy on a statutory footing to ensure victims' voices are heard and to encourage greater transparency and accountability for IOPC decision-making
*   Introducing new regulations to ensure police chiefs can automatically dismiss officers who fail background checks
*   Creating a presumption of dismissal for findings of gross misconduct and fast-track hearings for former officers

In January 2026, a government white paper on police reform also signalled intent to implement further changes, including enabling the appointment of an independent chair for the IOPC to strengthen governance and bring it in line with other arms-length bodies
The IOPC has welcomed the government's commitment to enhance accountability, scrutiny, and transparency

The 2025 Annual Stakeholder Research report found that "timeliness continues to be the primary source of concern," with only around 10% of stakeholders saying the IOPC does well at completing reviews and 9% for investigations in a timely manner
Police stakeholders, in particular, are critical of delays, citing negative impacts on officer welfare and trust in the IOPC

An independent review in March 2024 highlighted that the IOPC's investigation rate has significantly decreased, from investigating 1 in 6 referrals in 2018/19 to an projected 1 in 32 by 2025/26, which "could decrease public confidence in the system"
The review also noted that the IOPC faces significant financial pressures, with a projected 34% real-terms cut to its budget over seven years

The IOPC Director General Rachel Watson has previously called for "radical reform" to make the accountability system "more effective, fair and timely for everyone involved," including reviewing the threshold for misconduct investigations to ensure focus on those who genuinely behave badly, rather than junior officers making difficult decisions
Reform UK and its supporters argue that DE&I creates preferential treatment and "anti-white racism" within policing

Conversely, senior police figures and organizations like the National Centre for Diversity argue that DE&I is necessary to address existing systemic inequalities and build trust with communities that historically have less confidence in the police
They contend that any "two-tier" experience of policing is due to racial disparities in practices like stop and search, not the result of DE&I policies themselves
Regarding the IOPC, there is a general consensus among government, the IOPC itself, and other stakeholders that reforms are needed to improve timeliness, efficiency, and public confidence

The disagreement would likely stem from the specific nature and extent of those reforms, with some advocating for measures that might be seen as strengthening police powers and protecting officers (e.g., anonymity for firearms officers
